{
"title": "Can giant planets form by gravitational fragmentation of discs? Radiative hydrodynamic simulations of the inner disc region",
"authors": "D. Stamatellos & A. P. Whitworth",
"field_subfield": "Astrophysics: planetary system formation / protoplanetary discs",
"type_of_paper": "Numerical simulation study",
"executive_summary": "This paper investigates whether giant planets can form close to solar-type stars through gravitational fragmentation of protoplanetary discs. The authors perform radiative hydrodynamic simulations of the inner disc region (R < 40 AU) using the SPH code dragon, incorporating a newly developed method to treat the energy equation and equation of state, including radiative transfer effects, dust opacity changes, and the chemical/internal states of hydrogen and helium. Two cases are examined: (i) a disc heated only by an ambient background radiation field of 10 K, and (ii) a disc with additional heating from the central star (TBGR ∝ R−1). In both cases, the disc does not fragment. In the first case, the disc is Toomre unstable at ~30-35 AU but cannot cool fast enough (cooling time >~2tORB). In the second case, the disc cools fast enough but is not gravitationally unstable (Q >~1.5). The results corroborate earlier work by Boley et al. (2006) and Cai et al. (2007), despite using different radiative transfer treatments. The authors conclude that disc fragmentation is unlikely to produce giant planets around solar-type stars at radii <~50 AU. This work contributes to resolving contradictory results in the literature about disc fragmentation, which stem largely from different treatments of radiative transfer. The study uses 2×10^5 SPH particles and compares with analytic calculations of Hubeny (1990) for the vertical temperature profile. The findings have implications for understanding hot Jupiter formation, as fragmentation at large radii (>~100 AU) would produce objects unlikely to migrate inwards to become hot Jupiters.",

 { "The first condition is gravitational instability, quantified by the Toomre parameter Q <~1.": "The disc must be gravitationally unstable, i.e. massive enough so that gravity can overcome thermal pressure and centrifugal support (Toomre 1964): Q(R) = c(R) κ(R) / π G Σ(R) <∼1" },
 { "The second condition is that the disc must cool on a dynamical timescale.": "The disc must be able to cool fast enough for the compressional energy provided by the collapse to be radiated away." },
 { "Theoretical and simulation results on disc cooling are contradictory.": "Theory and simulations indicate that the disc cooling must happen on a dynamical time-scale." },
 { "Whether real discs satisfy these conditions remains uncertain.": "However, it is uncertain whether real discs actually satisfy the above conditions." },
 { "Hydrodynamic simulations have produced contradictory results due to different radiative transfer treatments.": "Hydrodynamic simulations have produced contradictory results about whether disc fragmentation can produce giant planets close to the central star, mainly due the different treatments of radiative transfer in discs." }

summary.executive_summary: This paper investigates whether giant planets can form close to solar-type stars through gravitational fragmentation of protoplanetary discs. The authors perform radiative hydrodynamic simulations of the inner disc region (R < 40 AU) using the SPH code dragon, incorporating a newly developed method to treat the energy equation and equation of state, including radiative transfer effects, dust opacity changes, and the chemical/internal states of hydrogen and helium. Two cases are examined: (i) a disc heated only by an ambient background radiation field of 10 K, and (ii) a disc with additional heating from the central star (TBGR ∝ R−1). In both cases, the disc does not fragment. In the first case, the disc is Toomre unstable at ~30-35 AU but cannot cool fast enough (cooling time >~2tORB). In the second case, the disc cools fast enough but is not gravitationally unstable (Q >~1.5). The results corroborate earlier work by Boley et al. (2006) and Cai et al. (2007), despite using different radiative transfer treatments. The authors conclude that disc fragmentation is unlikely to produce giant planets around solar-type stars at radii <~50 AU. This work contributes to resolving contradictory results in the literature about disc fragmentation, which stem largely from different treatments of radiative transfer. The study uses 2×10^5 SPH particles and compares with analytic calculations of Hubeny (1990) for the vertical temperature profile. The findings have implications for understanding hot Jupiter formation, as fragmentation at large radii (>~100 AU) would produce objects unlikely to migrate inwards to become hot Jupiters.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper investigates whether giant planets can form close to solar-type stars through gravitational fragmentation of protoplanetary discs. The authors perform radiative hydrodynamic simulations of the inner disc region (R < 40 AU) using the SPH code dragon, incorporating a newly developed method to treat the energy equation and equation of state, including radiative transfer effects, dust opacity changes, and the chemical/internal states of hydrogen and helium. Two cases are examined: (i) a disc heated only by an ambient background radiation field of 10 K, and (ii) a disc with additional heating from the central star (TBGR ∝ R−1). In both cases, the disc does not fragment. In the first case, the disc is Toomre unstable at ~30-35 AU but cannot cool fast enough (cooling time >~2tORB). In the second case, the disc cools fast enough but is not gravitationally unstable (Q >~1.5). The results corroborate earlier work by Boley et al. (2006) and Cai et al. (2007), despite using different radiative transfer treatments. The authors conclude that disc fragmentation is unlikely to produce giant planets around solar-type stars at radii <~50 AU. This work contributes to resolving contradictory results in the literature about disc fragmentation, which stem largely from different treatments of radiative transfer. The study uses 2×10^5 SPH particles and compares with analytic calculations of Hubeny (1990) for the vertical temperature profile. The findings have implications for understanding hot Jupiter formation, as fragmentation at large radii (>~100 AU) would produce objects unlikely to migrate inwards to become hot Jupiters.

Research Context
Disc fragmentation has been proposed as a mechanism for forming giant planets close to solar-type stars. Two main theories exist for giant planet formation: core accretion and gravitational fragmentation. Gravitational fragmentation requires the disc to be gravitationally unstable and to cool fast enough. The first condition is gravitational instability, quantified by the Toomre parameter Q <~1. The second condition is that the disc must cool on a dynamical timescale. Theoretical and simulation results on disc cooling are contradictory. Whether real discs satisfy these conditions remains uncertain. Hydrodynamic simulations have produced contradictory results due to different radiative transfer treatments.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether giant planets can form by gravitational fragmentation of discs in the inner region. The study focuses on the thermodynamics of discs and the probability of fragmentation. The authors hypothesize that fragmentation is unlikely in the inner disc region due to cooling or stability constraints. In the first case, the disc cannot cool fast enough to fragment. In the second case, the disc is not gravitationally unstable. The authors predict that fragmentation is possible at larger distances (>~100 AU) but not in the inner region. The predicted outcome is that gas giant planets probably cannot form close to the central star by gravitational fragmentation.

Methodological Details
The simulations use the SPH code dragon. The code uses an octal tree to compute gravity and find neighbours. The code uses adaptive smoothing lengths. The code uses multiple particle timesteps. The code uses artificial viscosity with α = 0.1 and β = 0.2. The code uses a second-order Runge-Kutta integration scheme. The energy equation is treated with the method of Stamatellos et al. (2007). The method accounts for compressional heating, viscous heating, radiation heating from the background, radiation cooling, and radiation heating from the particle's neighbourhood. The gas is assumed to be a mixture of hydrogen and helium. The equation of state accounts for rotational and vibrational degrees of freedom of molecular hydrogen. The equation of state accounts for different chemical states of hydrogen and helium. The effects of H2 dissociation, H0 ionisation, and the first and second ionisation of He are included.

Procedures And Architectures
The disc is simulated with a mass of 0.07 M⊙ around a 0.5 M⊙ star. The disc initially extends from 2 to 40 AU. The initial surface density follows Σ(R) ∼R−1/2. The initial temperature follows T(R) ∼R−1. The surface density profile is Σ(R) = Σ0 R−1/2 with Σ0 = 1.6 × 10^3 g cm−2. The temperature at R ≃1 AU is T0 = 1200 K. The asymptotic temperature far from the central star is T∞= 10 K. The simulations use 2×10^5 SPH particles. The first case uses a constant background radiation field of TBGR = 10 K. The second case uses radiation from the central star with TBGR ∝ R−1. The disc relaxes to a quasi-steady state within ~250 yr under low background heating. The vertical temperature profile is compared with the analytic calculations of Hubeny (1990).

Key Results
In the first case, the disc does not fragment because it cannot cool fast enough. The disc relaxes to a lower-temperature quasi-steady state when heating from the central star is ignored. The disc cools slowly under low background heating. Weak spiral arms form in the disc but they do not show any tendency to fragment. The disc is Toomre unstable at ~30-35 AU. The cooling time throughout the disc is generally >~2tORB. In the second case, the disc cools fast enough to fragment at radii >~20 AU. However, the disc does not fragment because it is not gravitationally unstable with Q >~1.5. The heating from the central star stabilizes the disc. The disc appears axisymmetric with no signs of spiral arms. The adiabatic index is γ = 5/3 outside ~10 AU where the temperature is less than ~80 K. Closer to the central star, γ = 7/5 due to the excitation of the rotational degrees of freedom of molecular hydrogen.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The results corroborate the findings of Boley et al. (2006) and Cai et al. (2007). The agreement despite different radiative transfer treatments is reassuring. The cooling time being >~2tORB explains the lack of fragmentation in the first case. The lack of gravitational instability in the second case explains the lack of fragmentation. The findings suggest that fragmentation is possible at larger distances (>~100 AU) but not in the inner region. Fragmentation at large radii produces mostly brown dwarfs and occasionally low-mass hydrogen-burning stars or planetary-mass objects. Planetary-mass objects formed at large radii are unlikely to migrate inwards to become hot Jupiters. The findings have implications for understanding hot Jupiter formation.

Contradictions And Limitations
The temperatures in the simulations are not high enough for molecular hydrogen to dissociate. Contributions from metals are ignored. The mean molecular weight µ is constant. The results are limited to the inner region of discs (R < 40 AU). The conclusions are based on two cases only. The results are compared with previous simulations and analytic calculations. The study does not account for the effects of stellar irradiation in the first case. The study does not account for the effects of stellar irradiation in the second case.

Claims
Disc fragmentation is unlikely to produce giant planets around solar-type stars at radii <~50 AU. The disc does not fragment in both cases. The disc cannot cool fast enough in the first case. The disc is not gravitationally unstable in the second case. The cooling time is >~2tORB within ~30 AU. The Toomre parameter Q >~1.5 in the second case. The disc cools fast enough to fragment at radii >~20 AU in the second case. Fragmentation is possible at larger distances (>~100 AU). The findings have implications for understanding hot Jupiter formation. The findings corroborate previous work.
The results are consistent with previous simulations despite different radiative transfer treatments. The results are comparable with previous simulations. The agreement is reassuring. The temperatures are ~15% higher than Boley et al. (2006). The temperatures are <3% higher than Cai et al. (2007). The findings suggest that the conclusions are robust.

Data And Code Availability
The computations were performed using the UK Astrophysical Fluids Facility (UKAFF). The code dragon is used for the simulations. The code has been extensively tested.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The simulation was repeated using a smaller number of SPH particles (5 × 10^4). The evolution of the thermal energy, surface density, temperature, Toomre parameter and cooling time were essentially the same. The profiles change only slowly with time as the disc cools quasi-statically.

Ethical Considerations
The authors thank R. Durisen, A. Boley and K. Rice for useful discussions. The authors acknowledge support by PPARC grant PP/E000967/1.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the internal energy of the disc for both cases. Figure 2 shows the logarithmic column density and cross-section of the density. Figure 3 shows the logarithmic temperature in the x-y plane and on the x-z plane. Figure 4 shows the Toomre parameter in the x-y plane and on the x-z plane. Figure 5 shows the cooling time in the x-y plane and on the x-z plane. Figure 6 shows the surface density and temperature at 5 instances during the disc evolution. Figure 7 shows the Toomre parameter and cooling time at 5 instances during the disc evolution. Figure 8 shows the disc temperature profiles vertically to the disc midplane. Figure 9 shows the logarithmic column density and cross-section of the density for a disc heated by the central star. Figure 10 shows the logarithmic temperature in the x-y plane and on the x-z plane for a disc heated by the central star. Figure 11 shows the Toomre parameter in the x-y plane and on the x-z plane for a disc heated by the central star. Figure 12 shows the cooling time in the x-y plane and on the x-z plane for a disc heated by the central star.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is that disc fragmentation is unlikely to produce giant planets around solar-type stars at radii <~50 AU. 2. The strongest evidence is that the disc does not fragment in both cases due to cooling or stability constraints. 3. The future path is to investigate fragmentation at larger distances and its implications for planetary formation.
